case.case_title: Seelawansa Thero and Two Others v Tennakoon, Additional Secretary, Public Service Commission
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, SC (FR) Application No. 575/2003, decided on 23 November 2004

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the cancellation of the petitioners' promotions to Class I of the Sri Lanka Teacher Education Service (SLTES) violated their fundamental rights under Article 12(1) of the Constitution, given that similarly circumstanced officers had been promoted earlier without cancellation.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioners argued that their fundamental rights under Article 12(1) were violated because they were denied promotion to Class I while nine other officers in similar circumstances were promoted in 1999 without cancellation, constituting arbitrary and discriminatory treatment.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the petitioners did not meet the mandatory requirement of five years satisfactory service in Class II Grade I at the time of application, unlike the officers promoted in 1999. The earlier promotions were made under different constitutional powers and circumstances, and the petitioners and the earlier promotees were not similarly situated for comparison.
key_facts: Petitioners were serving in Class II Grade I and applied for promotion to Class I in 2001.
Petitioners had only about one year of service in Class II Grade I at the time of application, not meeting the five-year requirement.
Nine officers were promoted to Class I in 1999 without meeting the five-year service requirement, but those promotions were not challenged in this case.
Petitioners' promotions were cancelled in 2002 on grounds of constitutional violation of SLTES rules.
The Public Service Commission's power to make appointments changed after the 17th Amendment, unlike the 1999 promotions made by the Cabinet under Article 55(1).

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that Article 12(1) guarantees equal protection of the law, not equal violation of the law. Unequal treatment must be based on lawful acts and valid classifications. Illegal acts done previously do not justify illegal acts now. The petitioners failed to meet the eligibility criteria for promotion and could not rely on the allegedly illegal promotions of others to claim discrimination.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that the petitioners did not fulfill the five-year service requirement at the time of application, unlike the requirements set by the SLTES minutes and Gazette. The earlier promotions in 1999 were under different constitutional authority and circumstances, and the petitioners had not challenged those officers' promotions as respondents. Therefore, the petitioners were not similarly circumstanced to claim discrimination under Article 12(1).
principles_established: Article 12(1) protects equal protection of lawful acts, not equal violation of law.
Classification for equal treatment must be based on intelligible differentia and rational relation to the objective.
Illegal acts previously committed do not justify repetition of illegality.
Petitioners must meet eligibility criteria to claim equal treatment.
precedents_cited: C.W. Mackie and Co. Ltd. v Hugh Molagoda, Commissioner General of Inland Revenue and Others (1986) 10 SLR 300
Gamaethige v Siriwardana and Others (1988) 1 SLR 384
T.V. Setty v Commissioner, Corporation of the City of Bangalore AIR (1968) Mysore 251
Ram Prasad v Union of India AIR (1978) Rajasthan 131
The Chief Commissioner v Kitty Puri AIR (1973) Delhi 148

outcome.holding: The Court dismissed the petitioners' fundamental rights application under Article 12(1), holding that there was no violation of equal protection of the law.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) was central to the petitioners' claim of discrimination in promotion. The Court's reasoning focused on the proper interpretation of equal protection under this clause, distinguishing lawful equal treatment from unlawful acts, which led to dismissal of the claim.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court held that Article 12 guarantees equal protection of the law and not equal violation of the law, emphasizing that illegal acts previously committed do not justify illegal acts now, and the petitioners failed to meet the eligibility criteria for promotion.
